nameStory: The Atlantic Razor gets its sharp name from its resemblance to an old-fashioned straight razor - long, thin, and with a blade-like edge. Like a barber's razor folded in its handle, this clam can quickly snap shut when disturbed, creating that distinctive razor-sharp silhouette that gave the entire family its memorable name.
description: The Atlantic Razor is a long, narrow saltwater clam that looks remarkably like a folded straight razor. These bivalve mollusks have thin, rectangular shells that are typically 2-4 inches long and much taller than they are wide. Their shells are usually whitish to pale yellow with a smooth, glossy surface, and they live buried vertically in sandy beaches with just their siphons poking up to the surface.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Distinctively long and narrow like a rectangle, much taller than wide, resembling a folded straight razor with straight parallel edges

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth and glossy surface that feels almost polished, with a thin, fragile shell that can crack easily under pressure

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Whitish to pale yellow or cream colored, sometimes with faint growth lines visible as subtle ridges you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Beach Position
idTips.description: Found buried vertically in sand like a buried knife blade, often with just small holes or siphon tips visible at the surface

idTips.label: Shell Movement
idTips.description: Snaps shut quickly when touched, creating a sharp clacking sound, and can burrow rapidly into sand when disturbed

habitat: Atlantic Razors live in sandy or muddy beaches along New England's coast, from the intertidal zone down to shallow subtidal waters. Look for them in protected bays, estuaries, and sandy shorelines where they burrow vertically into the sediment, often in areas with moderate wave action where the sand stays loose and oxygenated.

seasonality.spring: Best time to find them as storms expose shells on beaches and they become more active in warming waters. Look for the telltale keyhole-shaped breathing holes in wet sand.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when you can spot their siphons at low tide and find fresh shells washed up after storms. They're actively feeding and more likely to be near the surface.
seasonality.fall: Still findable but becoming less active as waters cool. Shells from summer mortality often wash up on beaches during autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Least active and hardest to find alive, but empty shells frequently wash ashore. They burrow deeper in the sand to avoid freezing.

funFact: Atlantic Razors are speed demons of the clam world - they can burrow into sand faster than you can dig with your hands, using their muscular foot like a turbo-charged shovel to disappear in seconds when threatened!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other razor clam species, but Atlantic Razors are more rectangular and less curved than jackknife clams. Remember: if it looks like a straight razor (rectangular), it's likely an Atlantic Razor; if it's curved like a bent knife, it's probably a different razor clam species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Atlantic' Razors, these clams are found in both Atlantic and Pacific waters under different names, which can confuse beachcombers using field guides from other regions. In New England, this is the classic 'razor clam' that most people think of when they hear the name.
compareHints: Since Atlantic Razors are the only Siliqua species commonly found in New England waters, compare them to their close relatives in the razor clam family like jackknife clams. Atlantic Razors are more rectangular and straight-edged, while jackknife clams are more curved and banana-shaped. Atlantic Razors also tend to be smaller and more fragile than the larger jackknife species.
